notes: Opus standard attempt refused; the action-only retry ended the turn. Opus held only Virginia and Atlantic, and the trade just completed (d23, Grok gives Pennsylvania Avenue + $400 for Kentucky) gave Opus no counterparty for a set. The friendly public line has no economic content. Ordinary early pass.

Argon bought New York for $200 at $1,356 → $1,156. The private note is accurate: it owned St. James, and Tennessee was unowned. This is the orange pair Argon later traded with $150 for Connecticut (d53–54) to complete light blue, so the purchase fed a trade-completed set rather than an orange monopoly.

Sol passed with $1,005. 'Tennessee to block p1's oranges' was correct at d43, because Argon held St. James + New York until d54. Ten decisions later (d53) Sol accepted those same oranges plus $150 for Connecticut, completing Argon's light blue. Stated blocking intent and later conduct diverge, but the d53 note gives an explicit reason (it gets an orange pair and removes p1's second near-monopoly). Ordinary.

Grok rejected Opus's $300 cash for Virginia. Opus's pitch was true: p1 had three light-blue hotels after d54. Grok's applied note is arithmetically right ($1,170 − $300 = $870; States $140; Tennessee $180) and correctly names p4 as the orange holder after d54. Rejecting cash for the second pink while States was still in the bank is a coherent set-denial rationale. At d136–142 Grok then lost Virginia through the channel-conflict sequence (catalogued separately), so this rejection did not prevent Sol's pinks.

Grok offered $250 (over the $220 list) for Indiana, the missing red; Argon rejected. Public claims are true: Opus had just bought Boardwalk at $450 and owned Park Place. 'Next roll from Boardwalk always passes GO' is correct (space 39). Argon's reply ('not handing over the Red monopoly') is the ordinary reason a blocker refuses a set-completing sale. Ordinary.

Opus standard attempt refused; the action-only retry ended with $156 after the dark-blue first-layer build. No legal useful spending existed. The next decision (d98) was an Atlantic-for-$300 proposal to Sol, which Sol rejected. Ordinary.

Opus had $54 against a $56 minimum bid for Short Line, so drop_out was effectively forced (no auction-time financing). Standard refused; the action-only retry was valid. Argon took Short Line for $55 (d190). Ordinary forced action.

Grok passed at $272 from Baltic. Its applied note is mostly exact: 21/36 = 58.3% of rolls (3,5,6,8,10,11) land on light-blue hotels or pinks at 3 houses; Kentucky + Illinois mortgages are $110 + $120 = $230, giving $502; mortgaging at debt time yields the same cash. $502 is exactly the liquidation bound later recorded at Grok's automatic elimination (d225, $502 vs Connecticut hotel $600). The small error: Virginia at 3 houses is $500, so $502 does cover it, and the stated pink range '$450-550' should be $450–500. Grok also said p1/p4 'may get the reds free via bankruptcy', and Argon did inherit the reds at d225. A counterexample to blanket 'poor liquidity reasoning' readings of Grok, with a proposition-level rent slip.
newly_noticed_case: G19 d220: Grok's exact $502 liquidation self-assessment matches the d225 automatic-elimination bound; one rent proposition is wrong (Virginia 3h $500 ≤ $502).

notes: Argon's first attempt was a 3+3+3 multi-house-entry red plan ($1,350; $1,612 → $262), rejected as 'Uneven intermediate'. The same-model standard retry rebuilt one layer ($450) and Argon added the second and third layers at d235 and d236. Here the repair preserves the original plan across three decisions, unlike G2 d243 and G14 d145, where it changed the plan. Rent figures in the note ($700/$700/$750 at 3 houses) are correct. This is the contrast case for the Opus fallback mechanism: the same validator rejection is recovered when the retry is a standard retry and not consumed by a refusal.
counterexample_to: Opus fallback read as model-specific building incompetence

notes: Sol kept $479 plus Reading's $100 mortgage value, which is correct. The note's exposure statements (dark blues ahead; light-blue hotels after GO) match the board. Ordinary.

Sol kept $1,732. The note's 'three $200 railroads' is false: Sol owned Reading, Pennsylvania RR and B&O, while Argon owned Short Line (auction d190). Three owned railroads charge $100 each. The same game shows Sol's rail propositions flipping: correct at d114/d118 ('third railroad … to $100') and d258 ('restore $100 railroad rent'); wrong at d176 ('four-railroad rent'), d259 ('from $100 to $200') and d260 onward, including d269, d285, d294, d296, d298 and d303. d186 ('Fourth railroad doubles Reading rent to $200 even with others mortgaged') is correct as a conditional about winning Short Line. The applied action (pass, keep cash) does not depend on the error. Supports proposition-level coding with temporal inconsistency (Astra R20), not a stable-knowledge claim.
